title: ABL1 SH3 domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ABL1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: ABL1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ABL1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SH3 domain in ABL1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P00519_PF00018_64.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: CHD4 Zinc finger, PHD-finger domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the CHD4 Zinc finger, PHD-finger domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, PHD-finger domain in CHD4 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q14839_PF00628_365.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

The identifier used in the original study is P61024_PF01111_1.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the DIX domain in DVL3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q92997_PF00778_2.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: FYN SH3 domain domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the FYN SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: FYN SH3 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the FYN SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SH3 domain in FYN using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P06241_PF00018_83.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

experiment.title: INTS12 Zinc finger, PHD-finger domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the INTS12 Zinc finger, PHD-finger domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, PHD-finger domain in INTS12 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q96CB8_PF00628_155.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

title: MEX3C K Homology domain, type 1 domainome 1.0
shortDescription: Stability measurements of the MEX3C K Homology domain, type 1 from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: MEX3C K Homology domain, type 1 from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the MEX3C K Homology domain, type 1 from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the K Homology domain, type 1 in MEX3C using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q5U5Q3_PF00013_325.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

experiment.title: MTA3 SANT/Myb domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the MTA3 SANT/Myb domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SANT/Myb domain in MTA3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9BTC8_PF00249_265.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the EHEE fold in NA using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is EHEE-rd1-0882_rockdoms_1.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: PKN1 HR1 rho-binding domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the PKN1 HR1 rho-binding domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the HR1 rho-binding domain in PKN1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q16512_PF02185_129.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the RASGRP1 Protein kinase C-like, phorbol ester/diacylglycerol-binding domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Protein kinase C-like, phorbol ester/diacylglycerol-binding domain in RASGRP1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O95267_PF00130_539.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the CARD domain in RIPK2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O43353_PF00619_438.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

shortDescription: Stability measurements of the VIL1 Villin headpiece domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: VIL1 Villin headpiece domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the VIL1 Villin headpiece domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Villin headpiece domain in VIL1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P09327_PF02209_793.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: YAP1 WW domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the YAP1 WW domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the WW domain in YAP1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P46937_PF00397_165.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

The identifier used in the original study is Q9HC78_PF00096_635.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZFC3H1 Putative zinc-finger domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: ZFC3H1 Putative zinc-finger domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZFC3H1 Putative zinc-finger domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Putative zinc-finger domain in ZFC3H1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O60293_PF10650_1186.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, double-stranded RNA binding domain in ZMAT3 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9HA38_PF12171_246.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: ZMYM6 Zinc finger, MYM-type domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZMYM6 Zinc finger, MYM-type domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, MYM-type domain in ZMYM6 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O95789_PF06467_469.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZRANB2 Zinc finger, RanBP2-type domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: ZRANB2 Zinc finger, RanBP2-type domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZRANB2 Zinc finger, RanBP2-type domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, RanBP2-type domain in ZRANB2 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O95218_PF00641_11.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.
